why: This repository is PUBLIC. Every tracked path is published to every clone, forever, and `git rm` does not un-publish history. The rules below are the classes of path that reached `main` once and must not reach it again: per-PR review residue, a directory named for scratch work, build output, an embedded git worktree, dev-home or secret material, an absolute path into the maintainer's real machine, and an office document carrying the custom properties its saving software stamped on it. Each is cheap to add by accident (a `git add -A` is enough) and expensive to remove.
how_to_fix_a_red: Delete the path, or move it somewhere the repo already publishes deliberately. Do NOT add it to `allowed` to make CI green unless you can write a rationale a stranger reading the public repo would accept — `allowed` is for paths whose name matches a rule but whose CONTENT is deliberately published, and every entry is reviewed as policy, not as a build fix.

path_rules.name: residue-name
path_rules.rationale: A path segment that IS a residue word, or a residue word followed by a delimiter. This is the rule that `temp-screenshots/` (80 files, 20.8 MB of per-PR before/after evidence) and `scratch/` (38 files, two sibling repositories' content) both broke. Delimiter-anchored on purpose so ordinary names that merely START with a residue word stay green: `template.py` and `bakeoff.py` do not match, and `tests/test_residue_name_rule_does_not_fire_on_template_or_bakeoff` pins that.

path_rules.name: residue-suffix
path_rules.rationale: Editor backups and the conflict-resolution droppings of `git merge`/`patch`. None is ever content; each is produced by a tool the contributor did not mean to commit from.

path_rules.name: build-output-or-cache
path_rules.rationale: Regenerable output. Committing it makes every clone carry a frozen copy that silently shadows a fresh build — the exact failure mode `src/personalclaw/static/dist` exists as a SYMLINK to avoid (see AGENTS.md, mechanical gotchas). `.gitignore` covers these; this rule is what catches a `git add -f` or a new directory the ignore rules do not yet name.

path_rules.name: embedded-repo-or-editor-state
path_rules.rationale: `.worktrees/` is the worst of these: `git add -A` stages each linked worktree as a GITLINK pointing at a local absolute path that exists on no other machine, and git warns that clones 'will not contain the contents of the embedded repository and will not know how to obtain it'. The artefact is a broken clone for every user, produced by the most ordinary contributor reflex there is (#3413). The rest is per-user editor and tool state that is not repo content.

path_rules.name: dev-home-or-secret-material
path_rules.rationale: A dev home holds LIVE credential material — `.local_secret`, `session_key`, `sel_hmac.key` — so committing one publishes working secrets, not just clutter. `.gitignore` globs these; this rule is the second lock, because the cost of one miss is not recoverable by deleting forward.

path_rules.name: dotenv-with-real-values
path_rules.rationale: `.env` and `.env.local` are where real keys live. `.env.example` is deliberately tracked and deliberately NOT matched by this pattern: it is the documented template and carries only commented-out placeholders (`sk-ant-...`, `xoxb-...`). `tests/test_the_tracked_env_example_carries_no_real_value` re-checks that claim rather than trusting it.

path_rules.name: internal-planning-draft
path_rules.rationale: Launch planning drafts are internal by their own declaration — all four files removed in this change carried a literal `**State:** draft, internal, not published` header while being served from a PUBLIC repository, and none was linked from any published page. One of them (`prechannel-arrival-baseline.md:15`) additionally published the exact scope set of a live personal access token (`gist, read:org, repo, workflow`), which tells a reader precisely what a stolen token would grant. The token itself was never in the file. This rule is a path rule rather than a content rule because the directory is the unit of the decision: `docs/launch/` is where launch planning is drafted, and drafting is not publishing. If a launch document is genuinely meant for readers, it belongs on personalclaw.dev or in `docs/guides/`, not here.

binary_size_rule.name: oversized-binary
binary_size_rule.rationale: A tracked binary is permanent, unshrinkable weight in every clone (no Git LFS here). Measured ceiling after the publication-hygiene pass: the largest tracked binary is `docs/brand/social-preview.png` at 352 KB, and `docs/screenshots/` tops out at 328 KB. 512 KB is one step above that measured max — the same 'one step above measured, forbid growth' shape the structural ratchets use. It would have red `temp-screenshots/graph-cap/before-after-harness.png` (1.80 MB), the single largest file the repo ever tracked. TEXT files are exempt: a lockfile or the CHANGELOG grows legitimately, and text diffs and compresses.

real_home_path_rule.name: real-home-path
real_home_path_rule.rationale: An absolute path into a real developer's home publishes the author's username and machine layout. This is an ALLOWLIST of placeholder home names rather than a denylist of real ones, for two reasons: a denylist would have to write the maintainer's username INTO the public repo to keep it out (self-defeating), and an allowlist reds an unrecognised name the first time it appears instead of only the names someone already thought of. The listed names are the complete measured set across the tracked tree — every one a synthetic fixture (`/Users/x`, `/home/u`, `/Users/dev`) or a dev-home path fragment (`/home/config.json`). Adding a name here is a claim that it is a PLACEHOLDER, not a person. `linuxbrew` and `lb` are claimed as placeholders on the same measured basis: `/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew` is Homebrew-on-Linux's canonical install prefix, byte-identical on every machine and named in Homebrew's own documentation, so it publishes nothing about this author; and `lb` is an unprivileged account that `scripts/fresh_install_validate.sh` CREATES inside a throwaway container (`chown -R lb:lb`, `su lb -c`) because Homebrew refuses to run as root — it is a fixture of the script, not a person's home. Four names are claimed on the same basis. `noor` is the invented persona whose Claude Code and Codex homes are the importer fixtures under `tests/fixtures/agent_tool_homes/noor/`: `/Users/noor` is the home that fiction's copied `~/.claude` still records its projects under, and the Codex rollouts and onboarding tests that quote those fixtures carry the same path. `old` and `old-name` stand for a PREVIOUS machine's username in the importers' 'a home copied from another machine still names that machine' example (`/Users/old-name/src/app` in `onboarding_import/sources/`, `/Users/old/src/app` in the changelog entry for that fix). `uploads` is not an owner at all: `/home/uploads/` is the synthetic uploads-folder prefix `web/src/pages/chat/imageAttachmentChips.test.tsx` builds its attachment paths from.

office_document_rule.name: office-document
office_document_rule.rationale: An office document carries more than its text: the software that saved it records who wrote it, who last changed it, their company and manager, the name, initials and account id of each revision's and comment's author, and whatever properties a document-management tool stamps on it, such as a sensitivity label. All of it sits in compressed XML parts that no text rule can read, so this rule opens every tracked office document (recognised by its content, so a renamed one is read too) and refuses one that carries custom properties, a sensitivity label in any form, or a person or organisation in an identity field. Identity fields are checked against an ALLOWLIST of placeholder values, for the reason the home-path rule gives: a denylist would have to publish the names it keeps out. Each listed value is a placeholder, not a person: the empty string; `Author`, which Word's remove-personal-information option writes in place of every revision author; `Unknown`, the first entry of every RTF revision table; and `python-docx` and `openpyxl`, the creator those libraries (both dependencies of this project) sign a new file with. `python-pptx` is deliberately absent: its template records a real person as the last modifier, so a presentation it made must have that field cleared before it is committed. A format the rule cannot read is refused rather than trusted: a legacy binary office file or mail item, a document that embeds a macro project or an OLE object, and a file whose extension names an office format it cannot open. The XML parts of a readable document are held to the home-path rule as well. Measured when this rule was added: one tracked office document, whose custom-properties part was removed in the same change.
office_document_rule.how_to_fix: An office-document finding is fixed in the document, never here: clear the named field (Word's remove-personal-information option or its document inspector does it on save), delete a custom-properties or label part together with its content-type override and its package relationship, or convert a legacy binary file to its XML format. Do not add a value to `placeholder_values` unless it names no person and no organisation: every value on that list is a claim that it is a placeholder, reviewed as policy.

allowed.rationale: Matches `residue-name` on its `debug_` prefix, but the word is descriptive of what it does, not a mark of residue: it is a documented manual on-host sandbox check (listed in `tests/README.md`) that prints the detected backend and confirms `~/.aws/` is blocked. Present since the initial public commit and referenced from the tests README. Kept broad-rule-plus-exception rather than narrowing the pattern, so the NEXT `debug_*` file that appears reds and forces a deliberate decision.
